findings.quote: is a carbon-based molecule made by living things, such as glucose
findings.problem: The definition of organic molecule fails at a boundary the lesson itself uses. Carbon dioxide is carbon-based and is made by living things in respiration (lines 80-82, 207-208), so by this definition it would be organic, but carbon oxides are classed as inorganic. 'Made by living things' is also the discredited historical definition: many organic compounds, such as synthetic ones, are not made by living things. A student using it would misclassify carbon dioxide as organic.
findings.source: Wikipedia, Organic compound, Definition section: simple oxides of carbon (CO, CO2) are generally considered inorganic; 'Historically, organic compounds were defined as compounds originating in living things', a definition no longer used. Checklist B01.

findings.quote: In the dark, or in cells without chloroplasts, a plant takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide.
findings.problem: General statement with a known exception. CAM plants, such as pineapple, open their stomata at night and take in carbon dioxide, storing it for the Calvin cycle the next day, so a CAM leaf in the dark has a net uptake of carbon dioxide, not a release. The same unqualified claim is in Core Concept: 'In the dark it takes in oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide, like an animal cell.' The trap teaches the rule as a correction with no limit, so a student would answer a CAM gas-exchange question wrongly.
findings.source: Wikipedia, Crassulacean acid metabolism: in full-CAM plants stomata 'open at night to collect carbon dioxide (CO2)'; 'The pineapple is an example of a CAM plant.' Campbell Biology, Ch. 10, alternative mechanisms of carbon fixation. reader-rules.md, Added after the Sol audit; checklist B01.

findings.quote: Plants do both processes. Respiration goes on in all living plant cells day and night, including roots, which need oxygen from the soil.
findings.problem: This paragraph has six sentences, over the limit of one to three. Other paragraphs also run long: the organic molecule/prokaryote/eukaryote paragraph (five sentences), the electron paragraph (five), the ATP-yield paragraph beginning 'One glucose gives only' (five), the anaerobic respiration paragraph (five) and the fermentation paragraph (five).
